title: On Winning Versus Succeeding
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay separates winning from succeeding, arguing that success is an internal contest -- achieving goals through effort and strategy -- while winning is an external outcome that follows from success rather than causing it. It uses John Wooden's philosophy of never mentioning winning to his players, instead judging them purely by effort and execution, as the central proof case for the argument, crediting this approach with ten straight NCAA titles. The piece warns that when teams substitute winning for success as their measure of worth, they lose the intrinsic satisfaction of striving and, ironically, become less likely to win consistently.
points: Winning and succeeding are distinct: people win after becoming successful, not the other way around.
Success is a contest against oneself -- setting goals, crafting strategy, and executing well -- that doesn't require anyone else to lose.
John Wooden never mentioned winning to his players, judging them instead by effort and execution -- a philosophy behind ten straight college titles.
When teams substitute winning for success as their measure of worth, they shift from learning and effort toward evaluating themselves by wins and losses alone.
Chasing winning directly, rather than success, tends to lower both personal satisfaction and the likelihood of winning consistently.
quotes: People don't need to win in order to succeed. They need to succeed in order to win.
Success doesn't require competition against anything or anyone. It is a contest against ourselves.
He asked his players to judge themselves by the effort they applied in every practice and performance to prove what they were capable of.
Wooden knew that winning follows success, and not the other way around.
Unfortunately, winning too often substitutes for what it means to be successful, and team members draw the wrong conclusions.
We only win consistently when we first achieve success. The best leaders let the wins come.
